blocks.p: Rei came back from Sumida in the worst of the afternoon heat. The walk from the station felt twice as long as usual. The cicadas in the trees along the road were so loud they seemed to be inside his head, and the shade under the railway bridge was no cooler than the sun. When he opened the door of the flat, the air inside was thick and still. And the ledger had grown while the flat stood empty.

It had never done that before. Every earlier entry had appeared in the small hours, while he slept. This one had come in daylight, while he was across the city with his hand on Iwata's thread. The timing was not lost on him.
The sulfur lay across the threshold exactly as he had left it, pale and dry. It told him nothing. It had been told to tell him nothing.

The thirty-fifth entry was short. It was in the leaning hand, the pen pressure that was not quite Gin's. It did not record a favour given. It recorded one offered and refused, and the refusal it named was Rei's.
R. would not set the weight down, it read, so the weight stays. We will try again when he is tired enough. He is nearly tired enough.... G.

So the count had always been a countdown. Rei saw it whole now, the way he had seen the timeline stand up and the spiral point at Kita. The ledger had never been a list of the saved with Rei standing outside it, taking notes. It was a list of the saved with a blank line kept open at the bottom. And that blank line had had his name on it since the first night he came to the door. Everything since then had been the Healer closing the distance between Rei and the moment he would be tired enough to be helped. The spiral. The favours in daylight. The note in his brother's hand. Iwata's tea, ready before he arrived. It was not racing him to Gin. It was waiting for him to come to it, exhausted and grateful. That was the only door it had ever needed anyone to walk through.

He should have felt hunted. Instead, for one clear second, he felt almost calm. A countdown, unlike a hunt, has rules, and these rules were simple and terrible. It won when he stopped. It won when he broke. The only thing it had no entry for was a man who kept moving while tired and refused to be grateful. That was his whole road now. Not to outrun the ledger. He could not. It wrote faster than he could read. His road was to stay, every hour, the one name it could not finish. Awake. Ungrateful. Still counting. Still his own.

He took out the folded note from that morning and laid the two side by side. The offer and the refusal, in the same patient hand. He was reading a conversation the Healer had been having with him for a week. Only one of them had been allowed to speak.

As the light turned orange on the balcony, Rei remembered a line from Gin's price list. The ramen place Gin always went to on Tuesdays charged eight hundred and fifty yen for the tonkotsu. Worth it. It did not matter what day it was. Rei was hungry, and it was Gin's place.

He walked there as the evening came down. The heat had eased just enough to bring people outside. An old man in a vest watered the potted plants in front of his house with a hose, and the wet concrete smelled of summer. Children ran past with sparklers that had not been lit yet, arguing about who would get the pink ones. In front of one house, a grandmother sat on the step beside a dish of burning incense and a plate of peaches, keeping her dead company in the cooler air. The smoke drifted across the street and Rei walked through it.

blocks.cap: The ramen counter where Gin ate on Tuesdays

blocks.p: Rei knew the place. He had been there with his brother a dozen times without ever understanding that it was a habit. A narrow counter, eight stools, steam on the window. He sat on the stool Gin always took and ordered the tonkotsu, the thick white soup made by boiling pork bones for hours until they give up everything they have. He ate all of it. The broth was heavy and too salty and very good. The man behind the counter looked at him for a moment, as if trying to remember where he had seen that jaw before. Then he went back to his pots. Nobody asked Rei anything. It was the first full meal he had eaten in three days.
On the way home he stopped at the 7-Eleven on Kita-jūjō Nishi. Gin had written about it in a margin, on page thirty-four of the archive, in the section on what practitioners carry.

doc.title: Gin's archive. Margin of page 34
lines: The 7-Eleven on Kita-jūjō Nishi has a staff member who always works Thursday nights who asks how I am doing and appears to actually want to know. I go there after difficult cases.
I do not think she knows what I do. I think she can tell when someone needs to be asked a normal question by a normal person.
I have never documented her name because I do not want to look at her the way I look at cases.

blocks.p: It was not Thursday. The young man at the register had dyed hair and did not look up from restocking the cigarette shelf. Rei bought a can of hot coffee he did not need and sat on the stool by the window for twenty minutes, under the bright lights, doing nothing unusual. Behind him a tired office worker was trying to decide between two onigiri. A delivery van idled at the kerb with its hazard lights blinking. The little door chime played its tune every time someone came in. Gin's page said this worked. And it did, a little.

doc.title: The Kombini Protocol. Ordinary Spaces as Stability Infrastructure
lines: Convenience stores at 3am are one of the most reliable stability recovery tools available. Bright lights. Ordinary transactions. Other ordinary people doing ordinary things. The kombini, where nothing significant ever happens, by design, is structurally cleaner than most spaces a practitioner encounters.
Eating a warm kombini meal. +3% stability. Standing at the counter, eating something hot, under fluorescent lights, while someone behind you debates which onigiri to buy.
Sitting in a kombini for 20 minutes doing nothing unusual. +2% stability. You do not have to try. You have to be there.
Your regular order at your regular place. +5% stability. The familiarity is the mechanic.

Near thin spots, active shrines, or suffering being ground, ordinary recovery is halved. You cannot kombini your way back from a deep clearance in Oji at 2am without first putting distance between yourself and the location.

blocks.p: Rei did not need the numbers. He could feel it. Something in him had come back a few steps from the edge, just from a bowl of soup and a stool by a window.

Rei finished the coffee and thought about the woman on Thursday nights who asked Gin how he was. She would be here on Thursday night. She would not know what to ask about. He hoped, foolishly, that she had noticed Gin had stopped coming.

Night came the way Obon nights come, lit by lanterns and full of the returning dead. Back in the flat, Rei did the things Gin's pages told him to do, in order, because order was something he could hold. He poured a salt line across the inside of the threshold, one continuous stream from the tub, with no gaps. He sprinkled iron filings along it, so that anything that forced the line would pay for it. He put Gin's heavy cast-iron pan on the stove, because a steel knife does nothing and a cast-iron skillet works, and because Gin had cooked in it every Sunday of Rei's life.

Then he lit the gas ring under the kettle with his lighter, and sat down with the lighter still in his hand. He turned it over and over. It was a cheap thing, scratched silver, and he had carried it so long that he no longer noticed he was holding it. He opened the archive at the section on inventory, and the lighter stopped in his fingers.

doc.title: Inventory and the Field Kit. Grounding Objects
lines: Every practitioner has one. An object that connects them to ordinary life when the veil layer is too loud, when they are close to the possession window and need something real to hold onto. The object is not magical. It is specific. The specificity is what makes it work.

Held during a stability crisis, +5% immediate recovery. Nearby during rest, +5% to total rest recovery. If you lose it, your stability ceiling drops 5% until it is recovered or replaced. Replacement takes one month. You cannot rush this.

The people I work with. Nakamura Aoi, ceramic bead bracelet. Kato Ryusei, a white chess piece. Katagiri Noa, small imperfect pottery bowl. Tsukishiro Haruki, dried flower, jacket pocket. Shimizu Ren, worn athletic glove, left hand only. Gin, unknown. The archive has a gap here.

doc.title: End of Inventory Notes. Personal Note. A Sunday. Quiet.
lines: Everyone has one. The ones who say they do not have one have one and do not know it yet. The object is not chosen. It accumulates.
Mine is not documented in this chapter. I wrote the entry twice and deleted it both times. Some things the archive holds back not because they are secret but because writing them down changes them.
Rei's is the lighter. He does not know that is what it is yet. He will.
G.U. Keys on the hook.

blocks.cap: Gin's keys, the object he signed at the end of every page

blocks.p: Rei sat with the lighter in his palm for a long time. Then he looked at the empty hook by the door, where Gin's keys had hung every day since Rei was small enough to be lifted up to reach them. Keys on the hook. Gin had ended almost every page of the archive with those three words. He had written that his own object was a gap. And then he had signed the gap at the bottom of every page for six years.
And on the night Gin went quiet, the hook had been empty, and the key had been lying on the walkway outside the door.

Rei did not let himself finish that thought. He closed his hand around the lighter instead. He felt something in him settle, very slightly, the way a small boat settles when someone steps into it who knows how.

He could not sleep yet, so he read. He read the chapter he had been avoiding, the one on reincarnation, because he remembered the night Gin had been writing it. Gin had been sitting at this table with a stack of very old files, and Rei had looked over his shoulder and asked what they were.

doc.title: Gin's preface, Chapter 12
lines: Rei came in last night while I was reviewing the Uedera family case files again, the fourth time I have gone through them this month.
He looked at what I was reading and said, those are really old. I said yes. He said, are they ours? I said, yes. He said, hm. And went to make tea and brought me a cup without asking.
He is sometimes very perceptive in ways that have nothing to do with the veil.
G.U.

blocks.p: Rei remembered the tea. He did not remember saying hm. He read on.

doc.title: CVD Entity Classification Reference. Chapter 12. Reincarnation. Research Classification. Contested
lines: Reincarnation is the only path that produces no detectable entity. The soul crosses, the self does not corrupt or dissolve, and it simply continues... inside a new life.
The CVD has seventeen documented cases of verifiable reincarnation over forty years. Its official position is unconfirmed hypothesis. That position has been unchanged for thirty-one years.

Karmic reincarnation. The soul enters a soulless neonate in a compatible family lineage. It does not arrive with memories but with orientations. Preferences, fears, relational patterns, ability profiles that do not match the family's genetic history.
Involuntary absorption. A dying person's extreme will to live creates a membrane vacuum that draws in a crossing soul. Neither party chose this. One body, two consciousnesses.
Children between about two and five sometimes describe places they have never been and people they never met. The memory window closes around age seven.

Multi-spectrum families show a progressive pattern across generations, each generation developing more paths than the previous, as if the soul carrying the capability is refining it over successive lifetimes.

blocks.p: The page was careful, the way all CVD pages were careful, but the idea underneath was simple. Sometimes a soul does not go on to the Font. It comes back, into a new baby, often in the same family. It does not bring memories. It brings leanings. A fear nobody taught the child. A talent nobody else in the family has. And in some families, each generation can do a little more than the last.

doc.title: Margin, G.U.
lines: The Uedera family files. Each generation stronger than the previous. Each generation developing more paths.

I am not concluding that the soul currently living as me has lived in this family before. I am noting that the evidence is consistent with that conclusion and that I find myself thinking about it more than is probably strictly necessary.
The family files are on the desk. The tea is cold.

blocks.p: Each generation developing more paths. Rei thought of his own two registers, the low one and the searching one. No file had ever measured them properly, because he had never let anything measure them. Gin had been sitting here working out whether the Uedera line kept coming back as itself. And then he had drunk the tea his little brother brought him and said nothing about it.

Rei put the archive down and sat with the two notes and the long torn strip of dates. He took his own pulse the way he would take a stranger's. Honestly. Clinically. Looking for the thing the Healer was waiting for.

He was tired. There was no use pretending he was not. The tiredness lived behind his eyes and in the two flat registers he had not let himself feel in days. The thing wearing his brother had read him correctly, the way it read everyone. That was its whole terrible skill. He is nearly tired enough. Nearly. The word was doing more work than Rei wanted it to. Nearly was a confession. It meant the door was not open yet. It meant there was still a margin. It meant that tonight, this hour, he was still the unfinished entry and not the closed one.

He did the only thing the countdown had no answer for, which was also the smallest thing. He decided to be tired and stay. Not heroically. He was too exhausted for heroism, and the Healer would only treat heroism as one more line it could help him across. He simply refused the rest, the way Iwata could not and the widow had never had the chance to. He kept the page open. He wrote nothing in it. He let the long night be long.

There was a difference, he understood now, between the rest the Healer offered and the rest Gin had written down. The Healer's rest was a knot. Gin's rest was a bowl of ramen on a Tuesday, a can of coffee under bright lights, a lighter turned over and over in a hand that did not know it was holding on. One of them asked for gratitude. The other only asked him to come back to his own life.

Somewhere north of Kita, his brother's body was sleeping a sleep that something else was dreaming. Somewhere closer, the ledger waited for the morning when Rei would be tired enough to be grateful. Between those two facts he sat awake, ungrateful and alive. It was, he understood, the only act of love the Healer had left him that it could not turn into a leash.

He would have to sleep soon. The body keeps its own ledger, and his was calling in its debts. But before he slept, he turned the strip of dates over. He started a new line at the bottom, on the blank the Healer had kept open for him. He did not write his gratitude there. He wrote the date, and beside it three words in his own handwriting, which did not lean. It was his own claim, staked on the only page the thing had been allowed to fill.
still counting.... R.

Then he lay down in the heat, with both notes within reach, the lighter in his fist and the salt line white across the door. He let himself be tired, on purpose and openly, an entry that refused to close. Outside, the lanterns burned for the dead, and somewhere a late train went by toward Akabane, and the city slowly forgot itself toward dawn. And the ledger, for the first time all week, held an answer the Healer had not written.
